text: Before you can do anything with real data, you need to know how to open a file safely. This lesson is about open(), the with statement, and why skipping with is a real risk once your script runs unattended.

open() returns a file object, and "r" puts it in read mode. The with block guarantees the file closes the moment you leave it, even if something inside throws an exception — without it, you'd have to remember to call f.close() yourself, on every single exit path, including error paths.

readlines() grabs every line into a list in memory — fine for a 21-line file, but a real problem for a multi-gigabyte export, because you'd load the whole thing before processing even one row. Iterating the file object directly reads one line at a time instead, which is the fix.

That line-dot-strip-dot-split-on-comma approach works on this file because none of its fields contain a comma — but it's fragile. A product name like "Tent, 2-Person" would get cut into two fields and shift every column after it out of alignment. Real CSVs quote fields like that, and a plain split doesn't know to respect the quotes.

"w" mode creates the file if it's missing, and completely overwrites it if it already exists — run that script twice and the second run replaces the first output instead of adding to it. "a", append, is the one that adds to the end instead. Mixing those two up is a classic way to silently destroy a log file in a real pipeline.
Next lesson tackles that exact comma problem head on: the csv module, which actually understands quoted fields and gives you back proper rows instead of raw text you have to parse yourself.
